prompt:
**(a)** Explain why $7,\ 11,\ 16,\ 22,\ \dots$ is **not** an arithmetic sequence. **[1]**

**(b)** The sequence $5,\ x,\ 19,\ \dots$ is arithmetic. Find $x$. **[1]**
markscheme:
**(a)** The differences are $4, 5, 6$; an arithmetic sequence needs a **constant** common difference. **(R1)**

**(b)** The middle term of three consecutive terms is their mean: $x=\dfrac{5+19}{2}=12$ **(A1)**

prompt:
In an arithmetic sequence $u_3=11$ and $u_{10}=39$.

**(a)** Find the common difference $d$ and the first term $u_1$. **[3]**

**(b)** Find $S_{20}$, the sum of the first 20 terms. **[2]**
markscheme:
**(a)** $u_1+2d=11$ and $u_1+9d=39$ **(M1)**. Subtracting: $7d=28$, so $d=4$ **(A1)**, then $u_1=11-8=3$ **(A1)**.

**(b)** $S_{20}=\dfrac{20}{2}\big(2(3)+19(4)\big)$ **(M1)** $=10(6+76)=820$ **(A1)**

**Common mistake:** writing $u_{10}=u_1+10d$. The $n$th term is $u_1+(n-1)d$ because the first term has had no differences added.

prompt:
**(a)** Write down the number of terms in $\displaystyle\sum_{k=10}^{40}(3k+1)$. **[1]**

**(b)** Hence find the value of $\displaystyle\sum_{k=10}^{40}(3k+1)$. **[3]**
markscheme:
**(a)** $40-10+1=31$ terms **(A1)**

**(b)** First term $3(10)+1=31$, last term $3(40)+1=121$ **(A1)**.

$S=\dfrac{31}{2}(31+121)$ **(M1)** $=31\times76=2356$ **(A1)**

**Common mistake:** counting $40-10=30$ terms. Both end values are included, so add one.

prompt:
A theatre has 20 seats in the first row and each row has 3 more seats than the row in front of it.

**(a)** The theatre has 25 rows. Find the number of seats in the last row. **[2]**

**(b)** Find the total number of seats in the 25 rows. **[2]**

**(c)** A larger theatre is built with the same pattern. Find the least number of rows needed for at least 2000 seats. **[2]**

A club's membership at the start of each year was:

| Year | 2019 | 2020 | 2021 | 2022 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Members | 120 | 133 | 145 | 158 |

**(a)** Explain why an arithmetic sequence is a reasonable, but not exact, model for these data. **[1]**

**(b)** Using the mean yearly increase, predict the membership at the start of 2026. **[2]**

**(c)** Comment on the reliability of your prediction. **[1]**
markscheme:
**(a)** The yearly increases ($13, 12, 13$) are roughly but not exactly constant. **(R1)**

**(b)** Mean increase $d=\dfrac{158-120}{3}\approx12.67$ **(M1)**; $2026$ is four years after 2022: $158+4(12.67)\approx209$ members **(A1)**

**(c)** It is an extrapolation beyond the data, assuming the same trend continues, so it is less reliable the further ahead we predict. **(R1)**
